title: Choosing a list, and how ConcurrentHashMap scales

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, why is ArrayList the better choice than LinkedList in almost all cases?

options.text: Its elements lie next to each other in memory, which suits the CPU cache
options.says: The page's Q1 gives cache locality first: the contiguous memory layout is CPU-cache-friendly, and it also costs less memory per element.

options.text: Its methods are thread-safe, so several threads can share it safely
options.says: The page's table marks ArrayList as not thread-safe, and says all non-concurrent collections are not thread-safe by default.

options.text: Its inserts in the middle take constant time, as later elements stay put
options.says: The page says ArrayList has O(n) insertion and removal in the middle, and names middle insertions in an ArrayList as a pitfall.

questions.stem: Per this page, how does ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8 and later) let many threads update it at the same time?

options.text: It splits its table into segments, each one guarded by its own lock
options.says: The page says segments and lock striping were the Java 7 version; Java 8 removed segments.

options.text: It locks the first node of one bin, and uses CAS when a bin is empty
options.says: The page says Java 8+ locks individual bins with synchronized on the first node, and adding to an empty bucket uses CAS.

options.text: It copies its table on a write, so that readers keep the previous copy
options.says: The page says ConcurrentHashMap uses per-bin locks plus CAS instead of locking the table; copying the array on each mutation is CopyOnWriteArrayList.

concepts: ArrayList is preferred over LinkedList in almost all cases, for its cache-friendly contiguous array, O(1) index access and smaller per-element memory.
Since Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap locks a single bin per update and uses CAS for empty bins, so threads updating different bins do not wait for each other.
